docs.title: How can we help?
docs.text:
BookReader is an EPUB and PDF reader with an agent that answers with quotes from the book and a review that comes back when it should. This help is organised by task: search above or take the door that looks most like what you are trying to do.

  • Start from scratch

    Install it, add a book, set up the agent and read your first chapter.

    Your first day

  • Read your way

    Table of contents, immersive mode, scroll, columns, themes and warm light.

    Read a book

  • Ask the book

    Select a passage and ask it to explain, cite or find where else the idea appears.

    Ask the book

  • Make it stick

    Turn what matters into cards, review them with FSRS or take them to Anki.

    Turn reading into review

  • Organise the library

    Shelves, smart shelves, reading status and clean metadata.

    Organise your library

  • Offline and on every device

    Install the app, read on a plane, sync with your own Drive and keep a backup.

    Read offline · Sync and back up

  • Bring an agent

    Connect Claude or another agent to your library over MCP, with per-token permissions.

    Connect an AI agent

  • Know what happens to your data

    Where your books live, what the AI sees and what you can export or delete.

    What happens to your data

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
This is the why, not the how. These pages are for understanding what BookReader does with your books and questions, and what to expect from the agent.

  • What happens to your data: where everything lives and what leaves the device.
  • How the agent answers: what it reads, how it cites and when it is wrong.

If you want to get something done, start with the guides.

Updated on 15 November 2026. Did this page help? Tell me: the help gets fixed where things actually get stuck.

docs.title: How the agent answers
docs.text: The agent does not "read the whole book" at once: it searches, picks passages and answers with them in front of it. Knowing how it works explains why it gets things right, why it sometimes finds nothing and why the citation is the part that matters.

docs.title: The path of a question
docs.text:
1. It reads the question and the context: the open chapter, the reading goal and the conversation template.
  2. It searches the book. BookReader keeps the text segmented on the device and uses that index to locate the passages dealing with the subject. It does not search the web.
  3. It trims. It does not send the whole book: it sends the passages that fit the budget for the question, prioritising the chapter you are reading.
  4. It answers and cites. The answer arrives with references to chapter and page. Tap one and the reader jumps to the passage.

That is why a small question works better: "what does it say here about X" finds more than "summarise the book".

docs.title: The goal changes the answer
docs.text:
The reading goal is not decoration: it decides what is relevant. "Why it matters" and "With numbers" use it to connect the passage to what you are trying to learn. Without a goal, those two actions ask for one before going on.

Notebook templates do the same for shape: a summary template asks for thesis and ideas; a study template asks for questions. The same question with another template gives another answer.

docs.title: Which model is behind it
docs.text:
• Demo: the house model, through our gateway, within a trial quota.
  • Your key: the provider and model you choose. BookReader talks to any OpenAI-compatible service.
  • Vision: explaining a figure or reviewing a sketch needs a model that accepts images.
  • Dictation: if you configure a transcription model, your voice goes to your provider instead of the browser's dictation.

The model changes quality, not the rule: the answer rests on the passages it cites.

docs.title: Where it can fail
docs.text:
• It cannot find the term. The book calls it something else. Try the author's words or Where else.
  • It cites well and concludes badly. It happens: the model interprets. That is why the citation is one tap away; if it does not support the answer, the citation wins.
  • A scanned PDF. There is no text to search. The page displays, but the agent cannot read it.
  • A very long book. Trimming favours the chapter; for the whole book, a specific question finds more than a general one.
  • Offline. It answers with the book's own passages, without reasoning over them; questions queue until the network returns.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not search the web or bring in outside sources.
  • It does not invent citations: if there is no passage, it says so.
  • It does not generate new artifacts offline or without a model.
  • It does not send your library anywhere: it sends the question and the passages it needs.

docs.title: What happens to your data
docs.text: BookReader's promise is short: your books stay on your device and the AI only gets what it needs to answer. Here is the detail, with no small print.

docs.title: Where everything lives
docs.text:
What Where Books (EPUB and PDF) The browser's storage on this device (IndexedDB) Highlights, notes, bookmarks, settings The browser's storage Cards, reviews, notebooks, conversations IndexedDB API key This device only Google Drive sync A private folder in your Drive (appDataFolder)

There is no account and no database of ours holding your library. If you clear the site's data in your browser, you clear that device's library: that is why backups exist.

docs.title: What the AI sees
docs.text:
When you ask, BookReader searches the book and sends the model:

  • your question,
  • the passages it found,
  • the reading goal and the template for that conversation.

It does not send the whole book by default, nor your library, nor your other conversations. If you attach a figure or the whole page, it sends that image.

With your key, the request goes from the browser straight to your provider. With the demo, it goes through a service of ours that talks to the house model; that is what makes trying it without an account possible.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
• Google Drive: data travels encrypted to a private folder in your Drive. The only server of ours involved renews Google's permission; it does not store your books.
  • BookReader Sync (Plus, coming soon): end-to-end encryption in the browser. The server keeps blocks it cannot read; it only decrypts what an authorised agent asks for, and only while the request lasts.

docs.title: What you can take out
docs.text:
• JSON backup: settings, highlights, notes, notebooks, conversations, decks, exercises and artifacts. Without the API key and without the book files.
  • Cards to Anki: .apkg or text.
  • Highlights and notes to Markdown.
  • The original book, from the book menu.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text: The app counts visits and activations (for example, the first deck) with Umami, without cookies and without personal or book data. There is no reading telemetry: it does not track what you read, for how long or where. Analytics never includes the part of the link carrying keys or the book you are reading.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
• One book: from its menu. The record and the file go from this device.
  • Everything: clear the site's data in the browser. Download a backup first.
  • Sync: disconnecting stops uploading changes; what is already in Drive or BookReader Sync stays there until you delete it from its panel.

docs.title: What I cannot promise
docs.text:
• A scanned PDF with no text cannot be searched or cited: there is no text to send.
  • A model can be wrong even with the passage in front of it. That is why every answer carries its citation: the citation wins.
  • If you lose every device and the recovery key for BookReader Sync, what was synced cannot be recovered. That is the price of nobody else being able to read it.

docs.text:

  • Sync and back up.

docs.title: Ask the book
docs.text: The agent answers with the book in front of it: it finds the passage that matters, shows it to you and writes the answer citing it. It does not search the web and does not make up sources; if something is not in the book, it says so.

docs.title: The quick way: select and choose
docs.text:
Select some text and the action bar appears. The top ones are the usual questions:

Select and choose: the bar carries the usual questions and, under “…”, the rest and highlighting. Action What it does Explain this Tells you in plain words, with a concrete example. Why it matters Connects it to your reading goal. What it means here The author's definition, not the dictionary's. Where else Looks for the same subject in another chapter. Strongest objection Argues against it: useful for reading with judgement. With numbers Turns the example into something measurable, when the book has data.

From the same bar you can highlight in one tap (with the last colour), add a note, copy, share a quote card, send the passage to the notebook or start writing your own question with the passage attached.

Two of them need a goal

Why it matters and With numbers need a reading goal. If you have not picked one, the app asks for it: it is what makes the answer yours instead of a generic summary.

docs.title: Asking by hand
docs.text:
Open the agent with ✦ (or ]) and type. You can:

  • Ask about the chapter you are reading or about the whole book.
  • Pick a reading goal and a notebook template for that conversation.
  • Ask it to answer in your language even when the book is in another: it searches the original and replies in yours, quoting the original passage.
  • Attach a figure or equation (PDF): select an area and send it with the question.

docs.title: Citations: you can check the answer
docs.text:
Under each answer there are citations with their chapter and page. Tap one and the reader jumps to the passage. That is the difference between "the agent says" and "the book says": if the citation does not support the answer, the place to check it is right there.

Every answer brings its citation and its page. The original passage is one tap away.

docs.title: Feynman mode: you explain it
docs.text: Instead of asking, you explain the concept and the agent plays sparring partner: it tells you what is missing, what is weak and what you got right, without giving you the answer first. Open it from the agent's menu.

docs.title: Speak instead of typing
docs.text:
Next to the text box there is a microphone (in Feynman mode too): record, release, and the text lands in the box. There are two engines:

  • With a transcription model (Settings → Agent → “Transcription model”, uses your API key): the recording is transcribed when you release, and it is far better with technical vocabulary and proper names; it doesn't cut on a brief pause. The recording bar shows a level meter, so you know it hears you.
  • Without one: the browser's recognizer is used. Live text, but it cuts on every pause and struggles more with jargon.

Transcription is biased with the book title and the open chapter: that is exactly where the proper nouns that would otherwise be guessed by ear live.

docs.title: The question at the end of a chapter
docs.text: With the HQ&A template active, when you start a new chapter the agent asks one recall question about the previous one. It does not give the answer: it is a check that what you read stuck. It only asks forwards and once per chapter.

docs.title: If the answer does not help
docs.text:
• "I cannot find that in this book": the term does not appear as typed. Try the author's words, or ask Where else.
  • It cites a passage and the answer wanders: make the question smaller. The agent does better with "what does it say here about X" than with "summarise the chapter".
  • No agent at all: see Set up the agent.

docs.title: Connect an AI agent to your library
docs.text:
BookReader can let an AI agent —Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Hermes or another MCP client— query your books: highlights, notes, stats, decks and book text. You decide what each token can see and revoke it whenever you want.

It ships with Plus

This connection is part of BookReader Plus and is still in testing. When it opens, the switch will appear under Settings → Data, inside the BookReader Sync section.

docs.title: What MCP is
docs.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard for letting an agent use tools from an app. Instead of copying and pasting passages, the agent asks BookReader and gets results with their citations, without leaving the conversation.

docs.title: Create a token
docs.text:
1. Settings → Data.
  2. In the BookReader Sync section, scroll down to Agents (MCP).
  3. Connect an agent and give it a name: it is how you will recognise it in the list and revoke it.
  4. Choose permissions. By default it can only read your books, highlights, notes and decks. You can also tick:
    • change decks and cards, and create summaries and maps;
    • read the text of your books;
    • organise the library (shelves, status, titles);
    • upload books.
  5. Copy the token right away: it is never shown again. The app also gives you the ready-made command for Claude Code.

docs.title: Revoke
docs.text: In the same list, each agent shows its last use. Revoke cuts access immediately. One token per agent: if one leaks, revoke that one and the rest keep working.

docs.title: How it is protected
docs.text:
• The sync server cannot read your library at rest: it is encrypted with a key only your devices hold.
  • To answer a query it decrypts only what the agent asks for, in memory, for the duration of the request.
  • Books cannot be deleted over MCP. Cards, summaries and shelves can be created and edited, with the write permissions.

docs.title: If the section is not there
docs.text:
• You do not have Plus or BookReader Sync is not active: the agents section lives inside that panel. BookReader Sync is not public yet; Google Drive is, but it does not expose MCP.
  • You changed device: the token belongs to the agent, not the device. Create a new one if you lost it; it cannot be recovered.

docs.title: Import a book
docs.text:
BookReader reads EPUB and PDF without DRM. There is no account and no book server: the file stays in your browser's storage, on this device. If you want it on another device, you sync later (or upload it again).

The library: your books, the one you are reading and the review due today.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• An EPUB or a PDF you can open without Amazon's or Adobe's app. If your book only opens in Kindle, it has DRM and BookReader cannot read it.
  • A scanned PDF (a photo of each page) displays fine, but it has no text: the agent cannot search inside it or quote passages. Fine for reading, useless for asking.

docs.title: Three ways to get it in
docs.text:
1. From the library. Open the shelf and press Upload files. You can also drag the file onto the window.
  2. From your phone. Open the file's share menu and pick BookReader (Android). On iOS, save it to Files and open it from Upload files.
  3. By double-clicking (desktop Chrome, app installed): .epub and .pdf files open in BookReader.

Several at once?

You can select multiple files in the upload dialog. They all join the queue.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
The book appears in the library with its cover (if the file has one) and its size. When you open it:

  • The table of contents comes from the book itself: in EPUB, from its table of contents; in PDF, from its bookmarks. A PDF without bookmarks reads fine but shows an empty sidebar. That is not an upload failure. Formats and limits explains it.
  • The text is prepared for search and for the agent. A large book may take a few seconds the first time.
  • Reading progress starts at zero and saves itself.

docs.title: If something is off
docs.text: Symptom What to check "Unsupported format" The file has DRM or is another format (MOBI, AZW3, CBZ). Only EPUB, PDF or a .bookreader dossier. It opens without a table of contents The PDF has no bookmarks. You can still read it. It opens, but the agent finds nothing It is a scanned PDF with no text. No cover The EPUB does not declare one; reading works anyway.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
• Set up the agent so you can ask the book.
  • Read a book to make it look the way you like.

Updated on 15 November 2026. Did this page help? Tell me: the help gets fixed where things actually get stuck.

docs.title: Organise your library
docs.text:
The library is the home screen: shelves on the left, books on the right. With a few books it hardly matters; with fifty, the difference between finding something and not finding it is how you organise it.

Shelves on the left, books on the right. Search and the status filter live on top.

docs.title: Two kinds of shelves
docs.text:
• Manual. You choose what goes in. New shelf creates one; you can nest them (for example Technical/Agents) and drag a book onto a shelf on desktop.
  • Smart. They fill themselves from a rule: status (not started, reading, finished), format, author, title, age, or membership of another shelf. New smart shelf lets you combine conditions. A book can be on several at once.

At the top you have the search box (Search book…) and the status filter. Search looks at title and author; status is picked from the dropdown.

Unshelved is not lost

Smart shelves by status cover every book. A book that is not on any manual shelf only means you have not filed it: it is still in the library and on its status shelf.

docs.title: The book's details
docs.text:
Open a book's menu (the three dots) to:

  • Edit title and author, if the download came with junk in the metadata.
  • Change the status: not started, reading, finished.
  • Share book: on a phone it opens the system sheet to send it to Kindle, email or AirDrop; on desktop it downloads the file. It can also be shared with your notes.
  • Export file, to get the original EPUB or PDF out.
  • Download the file if it lives in Drive or on another device.

Editing the details does not touch the book: the file and your notes stay as they are.

docs.title: Sharing a shelf
docs.text: From the shelf menu, Share shelf… creates a link. Whoever opens it sees the shelf and can save it; it expires, and you can withdraw it from the same menu. Remember the link carries your notes for those books: send it only to someone who should see them.

docs.title: Insights: what you actually read
docs.text:
Insights (in the library sidebar) counts reading time at a human pace: flipping pages to find something or leaving the book open adds nothing. You can look by day, week, month or year, by book or by shelf, and see:

  • Time read and words per minute.
  • Progress and days to finish.
  • Reviews, true retention and check-in questions on chapters read two weeks ago or more.
  • The load ahead, and the option to pause new cards if it piles up.

docs.text:

docs.title: Read a book
docs.text: BookReader is a reader before anything else. This is what you have while reading and how to make it yours; every setting is saved and applies to all your books.

docs.title: Open and get your bearings
docs.text:
Open the book from the shelf. Top left you have ‹ Library (back to the shelf without closing the book) and the contents and notes button. Top right:

  • Aa opens reading settings: type, theme and mode.
  • Full screen hides the bars (immersive reading).
  • Search jumps to search inside the book.
  • Bookmark page marks where you are.
  • … opens the rest: app settings and library.
  • ✦ opens or closes the agent.

The side panel has four tabs: Contents (the table of contents), Search, Bookmarks and Highlights. You do not need to select anything to ask the agent.

docs.title: The table of contents knows where you are
docs.text:
Each entry shows its page and the section you are in is marked. Books with several levels expand. Tapping an entry jumps to the passage, including in scroll mode.

A PDF with no table of contents

A PDF's table of contents comes from its bookmarks. If it was generated without them, it still reads fine but the sidebar is empty. Not a BookReader bug.

docs.title: Three ways to turn the page
docs.text:
• Pages: one page at a time, like paper.
  • Spread: two pages, if the screen allows.
  • Scroll: one continuous strip; handy for PDFs and for thumb-reading on a phone.

Immersive reading hides the bars so only text remains; they come back when you tap the screen or move the mouse. Press Esc to leave.

docs.title: Type and paper
docs.text:
In Reading settings:

Settings apply over the page, without closing the book: you see the change in the real text. Setting What it does Font and size The EPUB text. Not in PDF: the layout is printed and you adjust it with zoom. Column width A narrow column is easier on the eyes on wide screens. Line spacing Air between lines. Theme Auto (follows the system), Light, Sepia and Dark. Brightness and night light Lowers the white at night without inverting colours. Fit (PDF) Page, Width or Text. "Text" trims the white margins.

In PDFs you can also tint the paper: Grey or Night. Night inverts the ink, so photos and colour figures may look odd.

docs.title: Time and progress
docs.text: The book saves your progress and tells you how much is left: per chapter and per book, in reading time, not pages. The figure uses your real pace, so it ignores skimming.

docs.title: Bookmarks, highlights and notes
docs.text:
• Bookmark: marks a page in the bookmark list.
  • Select text to highlight it, add a note, copy it, share it or ask the agent. Explained in Ask the book.

docs.title: Shortcuts and gestures
docs.text: The full table of keyboard shortcuts and gestures lives in the reference: Keyboard shortcuts and gestures.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
• Ask the book.
  • Turn reading into review.

docs.title: Read offline
docs.text: BookReader is a PWA: it installs like an app and works offline with what you already have downloaded. It is not a cut-down mode: reading, highlighting, bookmarking and review all work the same.

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
• iPhone / iPad (Safari): Share → Add to Home Screen.
  • Android (Chrome): menu → Install app (or the prompt that appears when you visit).
  • Desktop (Chrome, Edge): the install icon in the address bar.

Installed, it opens full screen and the book you were reading carries on where you left it.

docs.title: What works without a network
docs.text:
Yes No Open and read books already downloaded Download a new book Highlight, notes, bookmarks Search the whole library Review cards and exercises Generate summaries, maps or new cards The agent with the book's passages Explain figures (needs a vision model)

Progress and cards are saved on the device even with no network; if you have sync, they upload when the connection returns.

docs.title: Asking on a plane
docs.text:
Offline, the agent answers with passages from the book itself (local search), with anchors to jump into the text. The question waits in a queue and is answered in full when the network comes back. That is recall, not reasoning: if it cannot find the passage, it says so.

Before you take off, in the agent's menu, Prepare for offline caches the summary of the whole book. It takes a couple of minutes and spends calls to your model, so do it while online.

The queue lives in the active conversation

Questions asked offline are sent when the connection returns in the conversation where you asked them. Questions from another book wait until you open that book.

docs.title: Books in Drive
docs.text: A book that only exists in your Google Drive cannot be read offline until you download it. In the book menu, Download. Books over 50 MB are not synced automatically: you request them by hand.

docs.title: Set up the agent
docs.text:
The agent is what turns the reader into something that answers. You have two paths and you can switch whenever you like: the free demo or your own key.

Everything about the agent lives in Settings → Agent: demo, provider, key.

docs.title: Path 1: the demo (zero setup)
docs.text:
The first time you ask for something, BookReader gives you a free demo: a quota of questions to try the agent with no account and no key. Nothing to switch on; if you want to see it or start it again:

  1. Open Settings (the gear).
  2. Go to Agent.
  3. Press Try the demo.

When it runs out, the app tells you and offers to add your key. The demo is for trying; for serious reading, use your key.

The demo goes through our gateway

To give you a demo without a key, the request goes through a service of ours that talks to the model. With your key, the browser talks straight to your provider.

docs.title: Path 2: your key (BYOK)
docs.text:
Bring your own key: you use your account with an AI provider and pay that provider for what you use. BookReader does not charge for the agent.

  1. Open Settings → Agent.
  2. Pick a Provider. There are presets for nan.builders, OpenAI, OpenRouter and Groq. With Custom, any OpenAI-compatible service works (a local model, a company gateway…).
  3. Paste your API key.
  4. Pick the model. If your provider is not in the list, type its id or refresh the catalogue.
  5. Save. The key stays on this device; it is not in the backup or in sync.

Vision and dictation models

To explain a figure or review a sketch, the model must accept images. To dictate with your provider instead of the browser, configure a transcription model. Both are optional settings in the same section.

docs.title: What changes with each path
docs.text: Demo Your key Setup None Provider, key and model Cost Free, within a quota Whatever your provider charges Privacy The request goes through our gateway The browser talks straight to the provider Limit It runs out Your account's limit Model The one the demo serves The one you choose

docs.title: If the agent does not answer
docs.text:
• "API key missing" or "Invalid API key": check that you pasted the whole key and that it belongs to the selected provider.
  • The demo ran out: add your key in Settings → Agent and carry on where you were.
  • The model does not respond or is slow: try another model from the same provider; long reasoning models take longer.
  • It does not understand a figure: you need a vision model.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
• Ask the book.
  • How the agent answers, if you want to know what it does with what you send it.

docs.title: Sync and back up
docs.text: Your books live on this device. To have them on another, or to avoid losing them when you clear the browser, there are two different things and it pays not to mix them up: syncing and backing up.

docs.title: Sync: the same data on several devices
docs.text:
There are two ways today:

  • Google Drive (free, available now). Your data goes to a private folder in your Drive. The only server of ours involved renews Google's permission; books and notes go from the browser to your Drive. That folder belongs to the app (appDataFolder) and is not visible in drive.google.com: do not look for it in Drive's interface.
  • BookReader Sync (included in Plus, coming soon). No Drive to configure and end-to-end encryption from the device. Not open yet: if you see it in Settings, it is in testing.

docs.title: Turn on Google Drive
docs.text:
Everything about backups and sync lives in Settings → Data.
  1. Settings → Data.
  2. Under Sync between devices, pick Google Drive.
  3. Connect Google Drive and authorise.
  4. Decide whether to sync book files too. Without this, the other device shows the details and notes, but you must download the book to read it.
  5. Save to Drive.

From then on sync is automatic. The same panel has Restore from Drive, Version history and the space left.

Over 50 MB

A book over 50 MB is not uploaded automatically. You request it from the book menu on the other device.

docs.title: Backup: one file with everything of yours
docs.text:
Settings → Data → Download backup (JSON). It includes settings, highlights, bookmarks, custom templates, conversations, notebooks, decks, exercises and Studio artifacts.

It does not include the API key or the book files. The key stays on the device on purpose: a backup you share should not carry your credentials.

Import backup merges: it overwrites what matches and does not delete what is left over. Restoring an old backup does not remove what you did afterwards.

docs.title: If something disappears
docs.text:
Do not touch anything yet, and in this order:

  1. Download a backup before anything else.
  2. Look in the other browser, profile or origin. Browser storage is per browser and per profile; two copies of the app can hold different libraries.
  3. Do not press "Clean orphan entries". It is meant for records without a file, and in the middle of a scare it is easy to make things worse.
  4. If the book is in Drive, check the sync panel's Version history: it keeps copies of the book file.
  5. If none of that explains it, write to me before uploading anything again: re-uploading a different file creates a new book and does not recover the old annotations.

BookReader has no telemetry: there is no central record of your library to look at. What exists, and what a diagnosis uses, is what stays on your device and in your Drive.

docs.title: Turn reading into review
docs.text: Reading is not remembering. BookReader turns the book into cards that come back just before you forget them, into notes you can read at a glance, and lets you take it all to Anki if that is where you live.

docs.title: The Studio: summary, mind map and infographic
docs.text:
Next to the cards, the book's Studio produces three notes that stay with you: they are cached per book, so you generate once and consult forever — offline, after the first time.

  • Summary: a TL;DR and key ideas per chapter, each with its citation to the passage.
  • Mind map: a navigable, branching map of the book's concepts; branches expand and the map grows on itself.
  • Infographic: a poster of the book —thesis, key ideas and a quote— ready to download.

All three are heavy jobs: they run in the background (you will see a progress chip; you can close the panel and keep reading) and if one fails, you retry it from the Studio itself.

docs.title: Where the cards come from
docs.text:
1. From the book's Studio. Open the book, open the agent and go to the Studio tab. Ask for Flashcards for a chapter, a selection or the whole book. The agent reads the text and proposes the cards.
  2. From a selection. Select a passage and send it to the notebook or create a card with its quote: the card keeps pointing at the exact page.
  3. From a deck you already have. In the library, Decks gathers every card deck, whether or not it is tied to a book.
The book's Studio: summaries, mind maps, infographics and cards come from here.

Before studying, review: you can edit the front, the back and the options. A bad card costs more than no card.

docs.title: Reviewing
docs.text:
In Decks you see what is due today. Review uses FSRS, the same kind of algorithm as Anki:

  • Each card comes back when the algorithm predicts you are about to forget it.
  • You grade with two buttons (Again · Good) or four (Again · Hard · Good · Easy). Two is faster and the algorithm works just as well.
  • The new-card limit stops a freshly generated deck from dropping 90 cards on you on day one. Cards you have already started always come in.
  • The streak counts the days you review; the "due today" counter says what is left.

The percentage is not a thermometer

FSRS schedules each review when it predicts you will be right about 90 % of the time. That percentage tends to 90 % by construction; what changes as you learn is the interval, not the number. The explanation says it without decoration.

A card from today's review: the answer in front and two buttons; FSRS decides when it returns.

docs.title: Exercises, in addition to cards
docs.text: The Studio can also build a practice matrix: rows and columns to fill in by comparing concepts, with citations. It covers what a card cannot: relating ideas, not recalling a single fact. Exercises live apart from cards and do not count as spaced review.

docs.title: Taking it to Anki
docs.text: In the deck, Export .apkg builds an Anki deck with your cards. There is also a text export for anyone who prefers to import by hand. Cards keep their page, so in Anki they still point at the book.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not invent cards for what is not in the text.
  • It does not send your cards to a server: they stay on your device (and in your Drive, if sync is on).
  • It does not replace reading. If a card does not ring a bell, go back to the passage: the link is on the card.

docs.text:
The facts you look up, not the ones you read start to finish.

  • Formats and limits: what BookReader opens, what it does with each format and where the ceilings are.
  • Keyboard shortcuts and gestures: keyboard and touch, in one table.
  • Sync and storage: where each thing lives, what sync uploads and the 50 and 100 MB ceilings.

docs.title: What it opens
docs.text:
Format Reads Table of contents Text for the agent Figures EPUB without DRM Yes, with adjustable type From the book's nav/NCX, with its levels Yes Yes, with a vision model PDF with text Yes, with zoom and fit From its bookmarks (outline) Yes Yes, with a vision model Scanned PDF Yes, as an image Only if it has bookmarks No Yes, with a vision model

And what it does not open: MOBI, AZW3, CBZ/CBR, EPUB or PDF with DRM (Kindle or Adobe), and anything that is not EPUB or PDF. A .bookreader file (a book with its notes, exported by the app) can be imported.

docs.title: EPUB
docs.text:
• The text reflows: you can change font, size, columns and line spacing.
  • The table of contents comes from the EPUB's own contents and keeps its levels. The "you are here" marker follows you down the chapter.
  • The page numbers in the contents are the reader's estimate, not the pagination of a printed edition.

docs.title: PDF
docs.text:
• It is a fixed layout: text does not reflow. You can zoom and choose the fit: Page, Width or Text (trims the white margins).
  • The table of contents comes from the bookmarks. A PDF printed from Chrome or Word usually has none: it opens fine, but the sidebar is empty. Not an upload failure.
  • With no text layer (a scan) you can read and look, but not search inside or quote passages. The agent has nothing to read.
  • Area: you can crop a figure or an equation and send it with the question. That uses vision, so it needs a model that accepts images.

docs.title: Sizes and storage
docs.text:
• Books are stored in the browser. A book of hundreds of MB takes a while to get in and uses device space; the browser may ask you to grant more quota.
  • Drive sync always uploads the data; book files only if you switch it on. Files over 50 MB are not uploaded automatically: you request them from the book menu.
  • A shared shelf link with the books inside is capped at 100 MB; without books, the link is light.

docs.title: Accounts and quotas
docs.text:
• Books and reader: free, no account.
  • Agent: free demo with a quota, or your key (you pay the provider).
  • Plus: €8/month when it launches; includes MCP, BookReader Sync and hosted AI. Everything else in BookReader stays free.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
A tutorial is a full journey with a clear start and end. It does not explain every option: it takes you from one state to another and teaches just enough along the way.

  • Your first day: from install to your first card, in one sitting.

Once you know your way around, guides handle single tasks.

Updated on 15 November 2026. Did this page help? Tell me: the help gets fixed where things actually get stuck.

docs.title: Your first day
docs.text: Twenty minutes, from nothing to your first card. You do not need to configure anything before you start: the agent comes with a free demo.

docs.title: 1. Install the app (2 min)
docs.text:
Open BookReader in your browser. On a phone, add it to your home screen: Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen; Chrome → menu → Install app.

Check: it opens full screen and you see the empty library with Upload your first book.

docs.title: 2. Add a book (2 min)
docs.text:
Press Upload files and pick an EPUB or PDF without DRM. If you do not have one at hand, any technical PDF you can already open in the browser will do.

Check: the cover and title show up on the shelf.

docs.title: 3. Make it yours (3 min)
docs.text:
Open the book and tap Reading settings:

  • Theme Light, Sepia or Dark.
  • Font, size and column width.
  • Mode Pages or Scroll.

Check: you are comfortable reading without touching anything else for the rest of the session.

docs.title: 4. Read a chapter (5 min)
docs.text:
Actually read, do not skim. If the book has a table of contents (Contents), jump to the chapter you care about. Notice the time left, at the top.

Check: progress moves, and if you close the book it reopens where you left it.

docs.title: 5. Ask about a passage (3 min)
docs.text:
Select a paragraph you did not fully get. In the bar that appears, press Explain this.

Check: the answer cites the passage and you can tap the citation to go back to the book. If the agent says it cannot find it, try a smaller fragment.

docs.title: 6. Turn the chapter into cards (3 min)
docs.text:
With the book open, open the agent (✦), go to Studio and ask for Flashcards for that chapter. Review the cards and save them to a deck.

Check: under Library → Decks the deck appears with today's cards.

docs.title: 7. Review tomorrow (1 min)
docs.text:
Come back to Decks tomorrow and press Review. Two buttons are enough: Again or Good. The card will return when it should, not when you remember to.

Check: the next day there is something "due today" and the streak starts counting.

docs.title: What you can do now
docs.text:
• Add a book and read it your way.
  • Ask with the book in front of you and check the citation.
  • Turn what you read into review.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Set up your key if the demo runs short.
  • Organise your library.
  • Read offline.
